title: Incentive Effects of Social Assistance: A Regression Discontinuity Approach
research_question: Do more generous cash transfer benefits reduce employment and labour supply among less-educated childless men, and do they affect their living arrangements and marital status? How large are these incentive effects when identified from a sharp age-based eligibility threshold?
data_description: The primary data source is the master files of the 1986 and 1991 Canadian Censuses (20 percent long-form sample), which permit observation of single years of age and yield roughly 1,500-3,000 observations per age cell for the target group. Key variables include current-week employment, weekly hours, weeks worked in the previous calendar year, earnings, unemployment insurance receipts, an 'other transfers' income category that mostly captures social assistance, marital and common-law status, and whether the respondent lives with parents. The analysis sample focuses on men aged roughly 25-39 who are high school dropouts without dependent children residing in Quebec, with men in the rest of Canada and the 1991 cross-section serving as comparison populations. The Labour Force Survey (1976 onward, monthly, 5-year age groupings) supplements the Census for time-series evidence around the 1989 policy change. Auxiliary checks use the 1985-1988 Survey of Consumer Finances.
institutional_context: Social assistance in Canada was funded under the Canada Assistance Plan (1967-1996), with provinces designing their own programs subject to weak federal conditions; unlike in the United States, childless single adults were eligible. Quebec's 1969 Social Aid Act set benefits according to family need, with a small earnings disregard and a 100 percent benefit reduction rate on additional earnings. A distinctive feature was that childless employable recipients under age 30 received sharply lower monthly benefits than those aged 30 and over: in 1989, $185 versus $507 per month, a gap of roughly 145 percent. Non-cash benefits such as medical and dental coverage did not differ by age. Recipients submitted monthly forms allowing administrators to verify when they reached age 30. The age-based differential was eliminated by the Act Respecting Income Security, which took effect on August 1, 1989.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: RDD — treatment = individuals just below income threshold, control = individuals just above income threshold; shock/instrument/cutoff = income eligibility threshold

key_variables.control: individuals not receiving social assistance due to income above threshold

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The receipt of social assistance negatively impacts employment and income levels.
key_robustness: placebo tests at other income levels
